item.title: Can AI Get You a Better Job? Is It Ethical?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Can AI Get You a Better Job? Is It Ethical?

Used properly, AI increases the probability of job success. But questions remain.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • AI doesn't create job opportunities or secure better offers; it improves how you compete for positions.
  • You can use AI to research, rehearse, and negotiate, not just to polish a resume or cover letter.
  • Some AI tools can be used against you, so pair automation with judgment and be aware of how employers use AI.
Source: Google Gemini/AI image generator

Will AI get you a better job? No, not by itself. Expecting AI to hand you a job is like expecting a calculator to put money in your bank account: It's simply not how the tool works. What AI can do is give you an edge in your job search, improving your odds of landing the job you want, provided you know how to use it and what to emphasize along the way. MIT tracked roughly 500,000 job seekers on a global freelance platform and found that those who used AI to help write their resumes were 8 percent more likely to be hired, received 7.8 percent more job offers, and earned 8.4 percent higher wages than applicants who got no such help (Wiles et al., 2025). The numbers aren't debatable. Using AI in your job search is not a nice-to-have; it's essential for success.

Presenting your credentials

Most resumes are written for humans but are first read by applicant tracking systems. Jobscan's annual audit of Fortune 500 career pages found that 489 of the 500 companies in 2025 used a screening system, a figure that has held between 97 percent and 99 percent every year since 2018 (Purcell, 2025). A resume that reads well but scans poorly will likely be rejected and never get the chance to impress anyone. These systems now go beyond keyword matching, evaluating resumes holistically, including how your self-portrayal matches company culture. LLMs synthesize content, infer intent, and make contextual judgments based on subliminal messages (Mao et al., 2023). AI benefits the screening process because it can quickly translate real experience into the language that applicant tracking systems recognize and reward.

Like people, AI tends to favor outputs that are familiar. Computer science research has identified the "self-preference bias," which is the tendency of large language models to favor their own generated content. This means screening systems favor resumes drafted with AI assistance over ones written by hand, choosing the AI-polished version up to 82 percent of the time (Xu et al., 2025). While holistic evaluation makes intuitive sense for finding the right hire, it magnifies the bias risk if an LLM systematically favors resumes that reflect its own generative style, reinforcing its own assumptions over time and depleting fairness from the assessment process. As Xu and colleagues noted, "this bias rewards access to specific generative technologies and penalizes those without it, even when applicants are otherwise equally qualified." Polishing your resume with AI means that when an LLM is the evaluator, you are 23 percent to 60 percent more likely to be short-listed than equally qualified applicants submitting human-written resumes.

Identifying opportunities

You cannot get a job offer if you can't find the job. Identification gets tricky with non-standard job titles, which vary among companies since there's no standard taxonomy. If your goal is to manage people as an HR generalist, you might need to search HR Manager, People Operations Manager, Talent Acquisition Partner, Employee Experience Lead, or Chief People Officer, among others. Miss one and you might miss the perfect job. AI can search for what you didn't know to look for: roles that match your skills but not your job title, postings buried deep in listings, or openings that fit a lateral move you hadn't considered. Unlike you, AI doesn't get bored, which is more than can be said for most of us by the second or third page of job listings.

Acing the interview

Mock interviewing is one of the best strategies for acing an interview. Unlike other role-play strategies, AI lets you precisely specify the personality, background knowledge, and attitude of the interviewer. You can structure the interview to test your knowledge, your cultural fit, or any other critical competency. Drop the company's strategic plan into the response criteria and test how your own beliefs align with the organization's. Or let the AI interviewer ask specific technical questions that help you calibrate knowledge gaps. An AI interviewer won't get tired of your answer, won't ask the awkward follow-up a friend is too polite to raise, and won't mock your ridiculous responses at a future gathering. A recent field experiment on AI-assisted recruitment found that candidates who went through a structured AI interview passed their final human interview at a 20-percentage-point higher rate than candidates screened by resume alone (Aka & Palikot, 2025). Why not increase your odds with practice only AI can provide?

Talking to decision makers

This is where AI gives you a decisive edge, performing grunt work in seconds that might take you days. Ask it to pull historical salary ranges for your role and region, compare benefit structures across offers, or draft the counteroffer email you keep rewriting in your head at 2 a.m. AI won't negotiate for you at the table, but it will prepare you by boosting your confidence and negotiation swagger, ensuring you walk into the final interview with hard data instead of a clueless grin. AI-supported candidates perform better in later human interviews and earn more offers than unassisted candidates (Aka & Palikot, 2025). Employers are using AI to find you. You should be using it to outmaneuver them.

One final note

AI hiring tools are not neutral, and job seekers should be aware of negative AI bias. One study tested three LLMs on more than 3 million resume-to-job comparisons and found the models favored white-associated names 85 percent of the time over Black-associated names, favored male names over female names by a wide margin, and never once favored a Black male name over a white male name in any comparison (Wilson & Caliskan, 2024). If a machine is judging you before a person does, it's worth remembering the machine has its own blind spots, none of which you can fix by trying harder. Newer models have endeavored to eliminate stereotypes, but bias mitigation remains an ongoing problem, since removing biased patterns without removing important assessment information is challenging.

Ultimately, AI provides low-hanging career support. While it won't get you a job, it will sharpen your resume, widen your search, coach your delivery, and arm your negotiation with data, not opinion. Just remember that the math AI uses is not always fair calculation, and the smartest job seekers use AI tools without relying on them for the entire job search process.

item.title: Is America Obsessed With the Failure of Mothers?
item.description:
Postpartum Psychosis

Is America Obsessed With the Failure of Mothers?

What "Yesteryear" and Lindsay Clancy say about the state of motherhood in America.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • People talk about both "Yesteryear" and Lindsay Clancy in a way that almost relishes in their failures.
  • Many women are trying their best to measure up to some “ideal motherhood” that does not exist.
  • Mothers should craft their own rules, in collaboration with the people and voices that they cherish the most.

Warning: This post contains discussion of postpartum psychosis and a case involving child death. There are intentionally no descriptions of the case; however, some readers may choose to avoid this topic altogether.

I am a therapist who has worked with postpartum psychosis in a variety of settings. I do not shy away from difficult topics. So why, when the Lindsay Clancy trial started, did I avoid this case with every fiber of my being? Because it showed me something I simply did not want to confront: America loves to watch mothers fail.

The Cultural Obsession With Mothers' Failure

This thought came to me when I was on a conference call with Postpartum Support International (PSI). Somehow we managed not to talk about Clancy—instead, we talked about Yesteryear. This has been the book of the summer. So many people I know have read it. I devoured it in two nights of breastfeeding my newborn.

The person I was meeting with, who had just read it, surprised me by saying, “It is so important for this organization; it is such a great conversation about postpartum.” It was not until that point that I realized that Yesteryear was not just a takedown of a "tradwife" influencer; its popularity extends beyond that. The book paints an amplified picture of two worlds: In one, liberal women lead lives focused on careers, miserable, putting the family and children on the back burner. In the other, where traditional values are on full display, motherhood and the maternal workload are done with seeming ease, and any chaos is carefully contained.

So of course we are also obsessed with Clancy. She is beautiful, educated, had three children she badly wanted, and everything still fell apart terribly. She had all the resources. She asked for all the help and did everything right—but the outcome did not change. What disturbs me most about these conversations is that they take a tone of fascination. People talk about both Yesteryear and Clancy in a way that almost relishes in their failures. They talk about how the psychiatric and mental health systems failed, how her husband failed, how she failed. They pull apart the details of her husband’s alleged affairs and look at images of her struggling to manage the children in an airport. In Yesteryear, the book focuses on the main character, Natalie, in a similar way: slowly losing grip on her children, her family, and eventually on reality itself.

In a post-Roe era where women have lost the right to choose motherhood, it is especially painful to see this obsession with the failure of moms. Every day I work with women who are trying their best to measure up to some “ideal motherhood” that does not exist. It is making them sick.

Modern Challenges and Impossible Expectations for Mothers

No matter where you stand politically, economically, or socially, motherhood is hard and is getting harder. Childcare costs are skyrocketing, and, for many, myself included, daycare costs more than a mortgage—just to get the privilege to work. If you are able to stay at home, it has become an aspirational lifestyle that puts added expectations on women. It is not enough to be a full-time mom. You must also make everything from scratch, have constant entertainment for your children (curated and plastic-free), and post everything online for the world to judge (but please, also stay off your phone. The kids are watching).

We can’t win. America knows this, and they are watching. That is the message as we watch this cultural moment unfold.

My advice as a therapist is this: Disengage from the dialogue. Know the game is rigged. Craft your own rules, in collaboration with the people and voices that you cherish the most.

Take the time and dig deep to understand your values as a mother and as a family. Step away regularly from the constant stream of parenting advice, news, algorithms, and carefully curated lives. Find other real-life mothers around you—the ones who have messy houses, whose kids are also melting down and acting wild, and who will tell you the truth when you ask how they are doing.

And above all, remember this: Motherhood is something you do, but it is not the entirety of who you are.
